title: Finding their way: Students’ fraction misconceptions and errors over two years of fraction learning

A speaker-centric motivation for the use of optional adjectives during language production
abstract: Speakers often make choices to alleviate planning difficulty during language production. We investigate the use of adjectives as optional words that speakers can use implicitly and strategically to provide extra planning time during periods of planning difficulty. Speakers described target objects in an array that either contained a different-colored competitor, so producing a color adjective was necessary to identify the target item, or did not have a different-colored competitor. Target items crucially differed in name agreement. Objects with high name agreement have a single, dominant label (candle) and are easier to produce than objects with low name agreement, which have multiple possible labels (coat/jacket). Speakers predictably produced a high rate of adjectives when describing high and low name agreement items in arrays containing a different-color competitor. However, when the array did not contain a different-color competitor, so adjectives were not necessary to identify the target, participants produced more adjectives preceding low name agreement objects. Further, when speakers produced adjectives, the duration of those adjectives were longer preceding low name agreement objects. We interpret these results as suggesting that the use of optional adjectives may sometimes have a speaker-centric motivation, to alleviate planning difficulty during language production.

title: Exploring avatar-mediated learning outcomes and motivation in the metaverse environment for sign language education
Identifying Indicators to Support Educational Attainment for Different Groups of English Learners in High School
abstract: This study examines a broad array of potential indicators for early warning and college readiness indicator systems (e.g., indicators made from English proficiency tests, grades, attendance, discipline records, and standardized test scores) for different groups of English learners in high school. Using data from 2008 through 2021 from the Chicago Public Schools, the study follows cohorts of students from eighth grade through college graduation, running exploratory analyses through logistic regression analyses and confirmatory analyses with omitted cohorts and machine learning methods. The study identifies ways of modifying indicator systems to better serve particular groups of English learners and to focus practices so that students are more likely to graduate high school and earn college degrees.

title: The Writing Identity Work of Youth: A Review of the Literature
abstract: Research in the field of writing and identity work argues for broader understandings of what it means to write and teach writing by foregrounding why and how learning occurs within a social, historical, and cultural context. Identity work as a research stance places value on the people doing the reading and writing and the contexts in which they situate themselves rather than considering text as a stand-alone product or writing as a decontextualized skill. Despite the breadth and depth of research in this area, there is not a comprehensive analysis of scholarly work on writing identity work, specifically focused on adolescents. To address the gap, this thematic, systematic literature review examines 91 articles focused on the writing identity work of youth. Findings show five common themes across the literature that illustrate how scholars define and describe how youth engage in writing identity work within a variety of contexts. Drawing directly from the findings in our review, we posit four principles of writing identity work to provide clearer and more consistent terminology and principles for scholars to draw on in the future.

title: Capturing moments, losing memories: A social photo-taking impairment effect.
abstract: Across four experiments spanning controlled laboratory tasks and a simulated art exhibition, we show that photo-taking reduces a nonphotographing companion's subsequent memory to a degree comparable to taking photos oneself. Mechanistically, we dissociate cognitive offloading from attentional disengagement. Instructing photographers to delete each photo immediately, thereby removing any expectation of later access, left both the self- and companion-PTIE unchanged, arguing against cognitive offloading as a primary driver. By contrast, preventing a nonphotographing companion from seeing the act of photo-taking with an opaque barrier abolished the companion-PTIE, implicating attentional disengagement as the causal pathway. Robust Bayesian meta-analyses estimated a reliable companion-PTIE with no meaningful difference in magnitude from the self-PTIE. These findings reframe the PTIE as a social phenomenon: The memory costs of ubiquitous photography extend beyond photographers to copresent others, revealing how everyday technologies reshape collective memory for shared experiences. title: The Falling Tone That Rolls Down the Hill and Gets Slumped: Vertical Mapping of Lexical Tones with Motion and Valence
abstract: While a growing body of research has identified the crossmodal correspondences between nonlinguistic pitch and vertical space, little is known about the non-arbitrariness of linguistic tones within the language domain. This study investigates the vertical mappings of Cantonese lexical tones (high rising vs. low falling) in two crossmodal domains: (1) spatial motions (upward vs. downward) and (2) emotional valence (positive vs. negative). Results showed that Cantonese speakers could reliably map tones based on pitch and motion trajectories (i.e., rising contour is upward, and falling contour is downward), but the vertical mapping between tones and valence (i.e., rising contour is positive, and falling contour is negative) was much weaker and modulated by vowels. In general, these findings suggest that lexical tones can be conceptualized and understood in the vertical dimension, even in the language where speakers do not talk about tones using spatially relevant terms. In addition, tonal iconicity, and sound symbolism in general, is differentiated according to the mechanisms in which they are grounded. Specifically, sound symbolism that relies on a direct structural parallel produces a more consistent mapping, whereas correspondence grounded in metaphorical mediation is more easily influenced by other linguistic factors. Thus, this research provides evidence for the sound symbolic nature of lexical tones, suggesting their conceptual mapping in tonal languages.

title: Exploring the impact of a GenAI-supported writing program on primary students’ writing motivation, engagement, and performance: A mixed methods study
abstract: Background The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into second language (L2) writing has attracted increasing interest, particularly in higher education. Yet little is known about its pedagogical value in primary education, especially regarding how younger learners’ writing motivation, engagement, and performance may change in GenAI-supported contexts. Aims This study investigates the impact of a GenAI-supported writing program on primary students’ motivation (i.e., growth mindset, ideal L2 writing self, academic buoyancy), engagement (i.e., cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive), and performance (i.e., opinion and content, organization, language use). Sample Participants were 301 Grade 5 and Grade 6 students from a primary school in Eastern China. Methods A mixed-methods approach was adopted. Eight classes were randomly assigned to either a GenAI-supported writing experimental group or a conventional writing control group. Writing motivation, engagement, and performance were assessed at pre-test (Week 1) and post-test (Week 9). Semi-structured interviews were conducted with selected students in the experimental group (N = 12) to explore their learning experiences. Results Quantitative analyses (MANCOVA and paired sample t-tests) revealed significant group effects on ideal L2 writing self, academic buoyancy, behavioral and emotional engagement, and two performance domains: language use, and opinion and content. Within-group analyses showed varying degrees of improvement across constructs. Qualitative findings highlighted GenAI's multifaceted roles in shaping these outcomes. Conclusions This study extends GenAI-integrated writing research to the primary level, demonstrating its potential to enhance L2 writing by supporting key motivational, engagement, and performance dimensions. Practical implications are offered for integrating GenAI meaningfully into primary-level L2 writing instruction.

title: Emotion regulation in children and adolescents with developmental language disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis provides the first comprehensive synthesis of research on emotion regulation (ER) in children and adolescents with developmental language disorder (DLD), based on 16 independent samples (NDLD = 1,616; ages 5-16). Individuals with DLD showed significantly greater ER difficulties than typically developing peers, representing a medium effect size (g = 0.563). This effect remained statistically significant, although reduced to a small-to-medium effect size, in sensitivity analyses excluding studies from the same research group (g = 0.317). Informant discrepancies emerged, with teachers reporting more ER difficulties than parents and children's self-reports. No clear evidence of publication bias was observed on formal testing; however, converging evidence from small-study effects, risk of bias analyses, and publication year trends suggests that the observed effect size may represent an overestimate of the true effect. These findings underscore the need for more rigorous, theory-driven, multi-method research to accurately estimate the magnitude of ER difficulties in DLD.

title: Four Decades of Stress, Depression, and Close Relationships: Lessons from Psychoneuroimmunology
abstract: Human psychoneuroimmunology research has demonstrated that stress, depression, and close relationships reliably shape immune and endocrine function in ways that matter for health. Across studies of examination stress, laboratory stressors, marital discord, cancer survivorship, and dementia caregiving, psychosocial adversity predicts more infections, weaker vaccine responses and faster erosion of vaccine protection, slower wound healing, heightened inflammation, and accelerated cellular aging. Depression also sensitizes immune function, producing larger inflammatory responses when individuals encounter stressors. Loneliness, low support, and distressed relationships can amplify stress reactivity and are linked to greater inflammatory and metabolic vulnerability, including postprandial inflammatory and endothelial responses. More recent work has extended these pathways to the gut microbiome and intestinal permeability (leaky gut), integrating microbial, neuroendocrine, and immune mechanisms. Collectively, the evidence supports a biobehavioral model in which social stress accelerates immune aging and increases risk for inflammation-related disease, while behavioral and nutritional interventions can modify these trajectories.

title: Reward selectively preserves relational structure in memory
A systematic review on the development of self-regulated learning
Behavior Change
abstract: Changing behavior is a central challenge in domains ranging from health and finance to voting and education. Drawing on decades of research from psychology and related fields, this review synthesizes high-quality evidence—particularly randomized controlled trials with objective behavioral outcomes—to identify effective strategies for changing behavior. We propose a unifying three-phase framework that conceptualizes behavior change as a process involving: ( a ) building motivation, ( b ) following through, and ( c ) forming durable habits. For each phase, we identify key psychological challenges and review interventions designed to overcome them. By organizing a large and fragmented literature within a coherent framework, this review aims to clarify when and why behavior change interventions succeed and to inform more effective, behaviorally informed policies and practices.

title: The Psychology of Question Asking: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Question asking, a foundational aspect of human communication, is an integral part of information-seeking behavior. We delve into the complex landscape of question-asking theories, exploring their diverse intersections with a myriad of fields—such as early development, artificial intelligence, and education. Synthesizing decades of research on question asking across different domains, we introduce the Question Asking in Information Seeking (QuInS) framework. QuInS provides a unified perspective on the iterative, dynamic processes that drive inquiry through question asking. We examine the early childhood origins of question asking, theories of inquiry, and the role of questions in fostering creativity, learning, problem solving, and social contexts. Finally, we explore how recent computational advancements contribute to formulate and empirically assess questions. Given the ubiquity of question asking in daily life, it is critical to elucidate its nature and mechanistic role in identifying and filling knowledge gaps. Such an endeavor will drive us to be more efficient, effective, and creative learners and question askers.

title: Natural disasters and early child development: Evidence from an earthquake
From stories to skills: The impact of narrative-based financial education on students’ knowledge and behavior
abstract: We study a low-cost, teacher-led program for 4th–5th graders in Brazilian public schools that embeds financial, fiscal, and civic concepts in short, comics-based stories paired with structured class activities. We evaluate a school-level randomized trial in Brazil’s capital Brasília covering 106 schools ( ≈ 13,600 students). Outcomes – knowledge and self-reported habits/beliefs – were measured with an age-appropriate instrument administered in person by an independent survey firm under exam-like conditions. Intent-to-treat estimates on a complete-case analysis sample show gains of 0.10 SD in financial knowledge, 0.06 SD in fiscal knowledge, and 0.06 SD in civic knowledge, all statistically significant and robust to alternative treatments of missing responses. We also find significant improvements in declared financial habits and beliefs and in civic beliefs. Beyond knowledge and beliefs, students also report greater school interest, more family interaction around money and public services, and higher future-self expectations. Placebo outcomes not targeted by the program, such as mathematics and monitoring of common goods at school, show no robust impacts. Monitoring data indicate that higher teacher engagement with the materials is associated with better student outcomes. Overall, the results indicate that culturally salient narrative media, delivered during regular class time, can measurably improve targeted economic and civic competencies at scale.

title: Mind the gap: The role of workers’ automation perceptions for the automation training gap
abstract: Technological advancements in automation are transforming job tasks and skill demands, raising concerns about the adaptability of the workforce. While reskilling and upskilling are widely recommended for workers in high-risk occupations, empirical research consistently finds an “automation training gap”: workers in occupations classified by experts as highly susceptible to automation participate in less training than workers in lower-risk occupations. Existing studies have primarily focused on employer-side explanations, but the role of workers’ own perceptions has received less attention. Using representative survey data for the Dutch workforce matched to occupational OECD automation risk indicators, we examine whether self-assessed job automation risk is associated with training participation and helps explaining the automation training gap. Our findings show that workers who perceive high automation risk have a 7 percentage-point higher probability of participating in training. Moreover, the negative association between expert-assessed automation risk and training is significantly attenuated when workers perceive their own job to be at risk. We also find that lower rates of self-initiated training among workers who do not perceive automation risk contribute to the overall gap. These results suggest that worker perceptions play a critical role in human capital investment decisions under automation risk. Policies aimed at increasing awareness of task-based technological vulnerability may enhance training participation and help mitigate skill mismatches in the evolving labor market.
